analysis.one_liner: Requires paystubs and contract wage rates, doubles penalties for unpaid wages, and funds wage enforcement grants.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Education and Labor Committee with 27 Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have amended federal wage law to require employers to give workers written disclosures of their pay rate, regular itemized paystubs, and a final paycheck within 14 days of leaving the job, and to honor any higher wage promised in an employment contract or union agreement. It would have doubled the damages workers can recover for unpaid wages (tripled in retaliation cases), extended the time to sue from 2–3 years to 4–5 years, barred employers from forcing workers into arbitration over wage claims, raised federal fines to as much as $10,000 per affected employee, and required the Labor Department to refer willful repeat offenders to the Justice Department for prosecution. It also would have funded $50 million a year in grants to community groups that help workers recover stolen wages.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers whose employers fail to pay them what they are owed — people shorted on minimum wage or overtime, required to work off the clock, misclassified as contractors, or denied their final paycheck. The bill's own findings cite research showing women, immigrants, and Black workers are hit hardest, with minimum-wage violations affecting 26% of surveyed low-wage workers in a single week. It also would have helped law-abiding employers who lose business to competitors that cheat on wages, and community organizations, unions, and legal aid groups that could have received federal grants to educate workers and assist in wage recovery cases.

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers to give workers a written disclosure of their pay rate and job classification when hired and when it changes, regular itemized paystubs showing hours, rates, and deductions, and a final payment for uncompensated work within 14 days of termination.

Makes employers pay the rate specified in an employment contract or collective bargaining agreement when it is higher than the minimum wage, closing a gap where workers could previously recover only the legal minimum.
Doubles the damages a worker can recover for unpaid wages (and triples them when the employer retaliates), plus interest, instead of the current equal 'liquidated damages' amount.
Extends the time workers have to sue over unpaid wages from 2 years (3 for willful violations) to 4 years (5 for willful), and pauses the clock while the Labor Department investigates.
Bars employers from making workers sign away their right to sue in court — including in a group action — as a condition of employment or in a pre-dispute arbitration agreement.

Raises civil fines for minimum wage and overtime violations to up to $2,000 per affected employee ($10,000 for repeat or willful violations) and requires the Labor Department to refer employers who willfully falsify records, steal wages, or retaliate to the Justice Department for criminal prosecution.

Gives workers the right to copies of their own wage records for up to 5 years within 21 days of asking, and if an employer's records are incomplete, the worker's own evidence of unpaid hours creates a presumption the employer violated the law.

Authorizes $50 million a year through 2023 in grants to nonprofits, unions, universities, and community groups to educate workers about their rights, help them file claims, and partner with enforcement agencies — a model the bill's findings credit with recovering more than $68 million in back pay for California janitorial workers.

analysis.who_pays: Employers, and especially those in industries with high rates of wage violations, bear the cost: new paystub and disclosure systems, fines of up to $2,000–$10,000 per affected employee, doubled or tripled damages with interest, a liability window stretched to 4–5 years, loss of forced arbitration, and potential criminal referral. Taxpayers fund the $50 million annual grant program. Compliant small businesses also absorb paperwork costs, though the bill would reduce the competitive advantage that wage-cheating competitors currently hold over them.

drawbacks.text: Every employer — including those already following the law — would face new compliance costs: providing detailed paystubs, initial and updated pay disclosures, and timely final payments, with fines of $50–$100 per employee for paystub violations and $1,000–$5,000 per employee for recordkeeping failures.

The liability exposure for employers grows sharply: a 4–5 year window to sue, doubled and tripled damages, and a rule that a worker's own testimony creates a presumption of violation that the employer can only rebut with 'clear and convincing evidence' — a high bar in litigation. Critics would argue these provisions invite expensive lawsuits whose costs ultimately land on prices, hours, or jobs.

The bill strips the Labor Department of discretion by requiring it to refer covered willful offenders to the Justice Department for prosecution, which could sweep in cases a prosecutor would otherwise decline.

The grant program authorizes $50 million a year in new federal spending through fiscal 2023, and grants go partly to advocacy organizations to monitor worksites alongside federal inspectors, which opponents would characterize as funding outside groups to police employers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall mostly on employers who are violating wage law or would face real compliance paperwork, while the benefits go to workers who today lose an estimated $15 billion a year to unpaid wages — and the bill's findings note that in some industries fewer than half of employers comply with wage and hour law. The doubled damages, longer filing window, and rebuttable presumption are aggressive by design and would raise litigation risk for borderline cases, but the same provisions respond to documented retaliation against workers who complain and to repeat offenders who kept violating after being caught. The heaviest burdens land on small and low-margin employers in low-wage sectors, which an honest supporter would acknowledge; offsetting that, compliant businesses gain from no longer being undercut by cheaters.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee in July 2019, never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and died when that Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on July 11, 2019 with 18 fellow Democrats as original cosponsors; the same day it was referred to the House Committee on Education and Labor.
A total of 27 House Democrats signed on as cosponsors over the bill's life; no Republican did.

The action history shows nothing after the committee referral — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, meaning it would have had to start over from scratch in a new Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers in industries where wage violations are common are better off: they continue to face only the current, lighter penalties and keep the ability to steer wage disputes into arbitration. Workers shorted on pay gained nothing.

for.name: Rosa DeLauro

against.name: House Committee on Education and Labor
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote during the remaining 18 months of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever took place, so the only measure of support is cosponsorship — 27 Democrats and zero Republicans — meaning the bill's fate was never tested on the floor.

industries.industry: Restaurants, retail, construction, janitorial, and other low-wage employers
industries.note: These industries, where the bill's findings say compliance with wage law runs below 50% in some cases, would face itemized paystub mandates, fines up to $10,000 per affected employee, doubled-to-tripled damages, a longer window to sue, and criminal referral for willful repeat violations — costs that come directly from practices that underpay workers.

industries.industry: Nonprofit legal aid groups, labor unions, and community organizations
industries.note: The bill's $50 million annual grant program would have funded these groups to educate workers, help them file claims, and join federal inspectors on worksite visits, giving them a stable new revenue stream tied to wage enforcement.

industries.industry: Payroll processing and HR compliance providers
industries.note: New federal paystub and disclosure requirements would create demand for payroll systems capable of producing the detailed itemized statements the bill specifies. This cost passes through employers but produces records that make wage theft easier to detect and prove.
